units.title: Completing the AA/AS Degree and Transferring

lessons.title: Finalizing the Degree Plan
lessons.summary: In your final year, the single most important habit is running a **degree audit** every semester instead of waiting until the end. A degree audit compares every course you've completed against your official **degree plan** and flags what's missing, so gaps in your **core curriculum** requirements or an unmet **prerequisite** show up while you still have time to fix them. Before you register for your last semester, confirm you've submitted your **graduation application** on time, since colleges have hard deadlines separate from registration. Watch closely for any **incomplete grade** or repeated course that could quietly derail your plan, and meet with your advisor early rather than assuming everything is on track.

keyTerms.definition: A report that compares completed and in-progress coursework against degree requirements to show what's still needed.
The official list of courses required for a specific degree, agreed upon with an advisor.
The set of general education courses (English, math, science, etc.) required of all students at a Texas public institution.
A course that must be completed before enrolling in a more advanced course.
The formal request submitted to the registrar to be reviewed for degree completion and conferral.
A temporary grade showing unfinished coursework that must be resolved by a set deadline or it converts to a failing grade.

practiceQuestions.question: A student runs a degree audit in the fall of senior year and discovers a required core curriculum course was never taken. What should the student do first?
choices: Wait until the graduation application deadline to see if it resolves itself
Schedule a meeting with an academic advisor immediately to adjust the plan
Drop out of the degree program
Assume the audit is wrong and ignore it
practiceQuestions.explanation: Catching a gap through a **degree audit** only helps if the student acts on it right away by meeting with an advisor to fix the schedule.

practiceQuestions.question: Why should students run a degree audit every semester instead of waiting until their final term?
choices: It is required to receive a diploma
It catches missing requirements while there is still time to fix them
It replaces the need for an advisor
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **degree audit** run early gives students time to correct problems before they run out of semesters.

practiceQuestions.question: A student has a hold on their account for an unresolved incomplete grade from two semesters ago. What is the biggest risk if it isn't resolved before the final semester?
choices: It could convert to a failing grade and threaten graduation
It will be automatically deleted after one year
It has no effect on the degree audit
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **incomplete grade** that isn't resolved by the deadline typically converts to an F, which can break a completed degree plan.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the purpose of submitting a graduation application?
choices: It replaces the need to complete the core curriculum
It formally requests that the registrar review and confirm degree completion
It is only needed for four-year universities
It automatically enrolls the student in transfer courses
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **graduation application** is the official trigger for the registrar to check a student's record against their **degree plan** and confer the degree.

lessons.title: Transfer Admission Requirements
lessons.summary: Four-year universities evaluate **transfer application**s differently than they evaluate incoming freshmen, so it pays to learn the rules early. Most schools set a minimum **transfer GPA**, often calculated only on transferable coursework, as a baseline for review, but many also use **holistic review**, weighing essays, activities, and major fit alongside grades. Every university runs on its own **application cycle**, with a **priority deadline** that can open scholarship and honors consideration months before the final deadline — missing it can cost real money even if the application is still accepted later. Before applying, check the school's **transfer equivalency guide** to see how your specific courses will count, so you're not surprised by lost credit after admission.

keyTerms.definition: The admissions application submitted by a student who has already earned college credit, evaluated differently than a freshman application.
The grade point average calculated only from courses that are eligible to transfer, which a university uses as a baseline for admission.
An admissions process that considers essays, activities, and major fit in addition to grades.
The full window of time a university accepts and processes applications for a given term.
An earlier deadline that unlocks the best chance at scholarships, honors programs, or housing, separate from the final admission deadline.
A published tool showing how specific courses from one institution will be counted at another.

practiceQuestions.question: A student wants the best chance at transfer scholarships at a university. What should they do?
choices: Submit exactly on the final deadline
Wait until after acceptance to apply for scholarships
Apply only to the honors program
practiceQuestions.explanation: Submitting before the **priority deadline** is usually required to be considered for the best scholarship and honors opportunities.

practiceQuestions.question: Why might a university use holistic review for transfer applicants instead of GPA alone?
choices: To weigh essays, activities, and major fit alongside grades for a fuller picture
Because GPA is not tracked for transfer students
To automatically reject students below a 4.0
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Holistic review** looks beyond a single number to understand the whole applicant.

practiceQuestions.question: Before applying, a student wants to know whether their biology courses will count toward their intended major at the new university. What should they check?
choices: The transfer equivalency guide for that university
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **transfer equivalency guide** shows exactly how specific courses will be applied at the receiving institution.

practiceQuestions.question: What does 'transfer GPA' typically refer to?
choices: The GPA from all courses ever attempted, including non-transferable ones
The GPA calculated only from courses eligible to transfer
The GPA after the first year at the new university
A GPA that only includes elective courses
practiceQuestions.explanation: Universities often recalculate a **transfer GPA** using only the coursework that will actually transfer, which can differ from a student's overall GPA.

lessons.title: Understanding Credit Articulation
lessons.summary: **Credit articulation** is the process that determines whether a course taken at one Texas public institution will count toward requirements at another, and understanding it can save a student an entire semester. The **Texas Common Course Numbering System (TCCN)** assigns a shared course number to equivalent classes across participating Texas colleges and universities, making it easier to predict how a course will transfer before you even enroll in it. Under state law, a completed **core curriculum transferability** block generally transfers as a whole between Texas public institutions, protecting students from losing general education credit. Still, individual **course equivalency** decisions vary by major, and choosing the wrong elective can lead to **credit loss**, where a course counts as a graduation requirement but not toward the specific degree a student wants.

keyTerms.definition: The formal process of determining how a course from one institution will be recognized and applied at another.
A shared numbering system that identifies equivalent courses across participating Texas public colleges and universities.
The state rule that a completed core curriculum generally transfers as a full block between Texas public institutions.
The specific determination of which course (if any) at the receiving school matches a course already completed.
When a completed course counts toward general graduation hours but does not satisfy a specific requirement in the student's new degree plan.
The transfer of an entire approved set of courses (like a completed core curriculum) as a single unit rather than course by course.

practiceQuestions.question: A student sees that a course has the same TCCN number at both their community college and the university they plan to attend. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The course will not transfer at all
The course is considered equivalent and should transfer as expected
The course only counts as an elective
The course must be retaken at the university
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **Texas Common Course Numbering System (TCCN)** exists to signal that courses sharing a number are treated as equivalent across participating schools.

practiceQuestions.question: Under Texas law, what typically happens to a student's completed core curriculum when they transfer between two Texas public institutions?
choices: It must be repeated in full at the new school
Only elective courses within it transfer
It transfers as a complete block
It transfers only if the student has a 3.5 GPA or higher
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Core curriculum transferability** rules generally allow a completed core to move as a **block transfer** rather than being evaluated course by course.

practiceQuestions.question: A student took a course that satisfies general graduation hours at their new university but does not count toward their specific major requirements. This is an example of what?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Credit loss** happens when a course transfers in some form but doesn't fulfill the specific requirement a student needs.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the best way for a student to avoid credit loss before choosing an elective?
choices: Assume all courses transfer the same way
Check course equivalency and articulation information for the intended major before enrolling
Only take courses recommended by friends
Wait until after transferring to check
practiceQuestions.explanation: Checking **course equivalency** through **credit articulation** resources before enrolling prevents unpleasant surprises after transfer.

lessons.title: Advanced Scholarship Essay Strategy
lessons.summary: By senior year, most students have written at least one scholarship essay — the goal now is to stop submitting a **generic essay** and start writing a **tailored response** for each committee. Every scholarship has a **committee intent** behind its prompt: a values-based scholarship wants evidence of character, while a STEM scholarship wants evidence of persistence in technical work. Strong essays use **specificity** — real names, numbers, and moments — instead of broad statements, and they follow **show-don't-tell** by demonstrating a quality through a scene rather than simply claiming it. The strongest essays also build a clear **narrative arc**, showing where the student started, what challenged them, and how they changed, so the reader remembers the story long after reading dozens of others.

keyTerms.definition: An essay written specifically to answer a scholarship's actual prompt and values, not reused word-for-word from another application.
The underlying quality or value a scholarship committee is trying to identify through its essay prompt.
The structure of a story showing a starting point, a challenge, and a change or growth.
The use of concrete details, names, numbers, and moments instead of vague generalizations.
An essay that could be submitted to almost any scholarship without changes, usually because it lacks specific details tied to that prompt.
A writing technique that demonstrates a quality through a specific scene or example instead of just stating it.

practiceQuestions.question: A scholarship prompt asks, 'Describe a time you showed leadership in your community.' A student writes: 'I am a natural leader and always help others.' What is missing?
choices: Specific details and a real example that show rather than tell
practiceQuestions.explanation: Without **specificity** and a real scene, the essay tells the reader a quality instead of using **show-don't-tell** to prove it.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is submitting the same generic essay to every scholarship a weak strategy?
choices: It saves time and is always the best approach
It fails to address each committee's specific intent behind their prompt
Scholarship committees never read essays closely
It guarantees rejection from every scholarship
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **generic essay** ignores the **committee intent** unique to each scholarship, making it less persuasive to that specific reader.

practiceQuestions.question: A scholarship for future nurses asks applicants to describe overcoming a challenge. What should the student prioritize in their response?
choices: A challenge unrelated to healthcare or caregiving
A challenge that connects to resilience, empathy, or growth relevant to nursing
The longest possible essay regardless of topic
Listing every award they have won
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reading the **committee intent** behind a nursing scholarship means connecting the challenge to qualities like resilience and empathy that matter in that field.

practiceQuestions.question: What does a strong narrative arc in a scholarship essay typically include?
choices: A list of accomplishments with no connecting story
A starting point, a challenge, and evidence of growth or change
Only future goals with no personal history
A summary of the student's resume
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **narrative arc** gives the reader a clear before-and-after, showing genuine growth rather than a flat list of facts.

lessons.title: Interview Skills for Scholarships and Programs
lessons.summary: Some scholarships and selective programs add an interview stage, and preparation matters as much as the application itself. Every student should have a 30-second **elevator pitch** ready that summarizes who they are, what they've done, and what they're pursuing next. Interviewers often ask a **behavioral question**, like 'Tell me about a time you failed,' expecting a specific story rather than a general answer. During the interview, **active listening** — pausing, nodding, and responding directly to what was asked — builds **rapport** with the panel and shows genuine engagement. **Professional presentation**, from appropriate dress to a firm handshake and eye contact, sets the tone before a single word is spoken, and sending a brief **follow-up thank-you** afterward reinforces a strong impression.

keyTerms.definition: A short, prepared summary (about 30 seconds) introducing who you are, what you've done, and what you're pursuing.
An interview question that asks for a specific past example, such as 'Tell me about a time you overcame a setback.'
Fully focusing on and responding to what the interviewer says rather than just waiting for a turn to speak.
The overall impression created by dress, posture, handshake, and eye contact during an interview.
A brief message sent after an interview to express appreciation and reinforce a positive impression.
A sense of connection and mutual understanding built between two people during a conversation.

practiceQuestions.question: An interviewer asks, 'Tell me about a time you failed and what you learned.' What kind of question is this?
choices: A behavioral question requiring a specific example
A trick question with no real answer
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **behavioral question** asks for a real, specific story rather than a general statement.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of preparing an elevator pitch before a scholarship interview?
choices: To memorize a script and read it word for word
To have a clear, ready summary of yourself for when the interview opens
To avoid answering any follow-up questions
To replace the need for a resume
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **elevator pitch** gives a student a confident, concise opening instead of stumbling through an unprepared introduction.

practiceQuestions.question: During an interview, a student pauses to make sure they understood the question, then answers it directly instead of giving a rehearsed unrelated answer. This demonstrates which skill?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Active listening** means genuinely engaging with the question asked instead of reciting a memorized response.

practiceQuestions.question: What is an appropriate step to take within a day or two after a scholarship interview?
choices: Contact the panel repeatedly to ask for a decision
Send a brief follow-up thank-you message
Ask for the interview to be redone
Do nothing and wait for results
practiceQuestions.explanation: A short **follow-up thank-you** shows professionalism and keeps a positive impression fresh with the panel.

lessons.title: Tracking Deadlines and Building a Resume
lessons.summary: Seniors juggling multiple scholarships need a system, not memory alone. A **master deadline tracker** — one spreadsheet listing every scholarship, its requirements, and its due date — prevents missing a deadline because it was scattered across emails. Alongside it, an **application inventory** lists what materials each one needs, like transcripts or letters of recommendation, so nothing is requested last minute. The **activities resume** itself should do more than list activities; it should build a **growth narrative**, showing how a student's role and impact expanded from ninth grade through senior year. Because some scholarships require **supplemental materials** like a portfolio or extra essay, a **priority ranking** of which applications matter most helps a student spend limited time wisely.

keyTerms.definition: A single organized list (spreadsheet or calendar) of every application and its due date, used to avoid missed deadlines.
A checklist of the specific materials (transcripts, letters, essays) required for each individual application.
A document listing a student's extracurricular activities, leadership roles, and accomplishments, usually organized by category or year.
The way an activities resume shows increasing responsibility or impact over time, rather than a static list.
Additional items beyond the base application, such as a portfolio, extra essay, or writing sample, required by some scholarships.
An ordering of applications by importance or likelihood of success, used to allocate limited time effectively.

practiceQuestions.question: A student is applying to six scholarships with different deadlines and requirements. What is the best first step to stay organized?
choices: Rely on memory and check email as reminders come in
Build a master deadline tracker listing every scholarship and its due date
Apply to only one scholarship at a time in random order
Wait until two weeks before each deadline to start
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **master deadline tracker** centralizes every requirement and date so nothing is missed or duplicated.

practiceQuestions.question: What makes an activities resume stronger than a simple list of clubs joined?
choices: Listing as many clubs as possible with no detail
Showing a growth narrative of increasing responsibility over four years
Only including activities from senior year
Removing all leadership roles to appear humble
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **growth narrative** shows a reader how a student's impact and responsibility expanded over time, which is more persuasive than a flat list.

practiceQuestions.question: A scholarship requires two letters of recommendation and a transcript in addition to the main application. Where should a student track this?
choices: Nowhere, it is easy to remember
In an application inventory listing required materials for each scholarship
Only in the recommendation letter itself
In a text message to a friend
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **application inventory** ensures every required document is requested and submitted before the deadline.

practiceQuestions.question: A student has limited time and many applications. What should they do to use their time most effectively?
choices: Apply to every scholarship equally regardless of fit or odds
Create a priority ranking based on fit, deadline, and likelihood of success
Only apply to the scholarship with the largest dollar amount
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **priority ranking** helps a student focus limited time on the applications most likely to pay off.

lessons.title: Personal Budgeting for College
lessons.summary: Many first-year students underestimate what college actually costs because they only think about tuition. The true **cost of attendance** includes tuition, fees, housing, food, books, transportation, and personal expenses, and financial aid offices publish this full number for a reason. Building a working **budget** starts with separating **fixed expense**s, like rent, which stay the same each month, from **variable expense**s, like food, which change. A common first-year mistake is spending freely early in the semester and running short later, which can lead to an **overdraft** and unnecessary bank fees. Setting aside even a small **emergency fund** — money not touched for everyday spending — helps cover a surprise cost like a car repair without derailing the whole budget.

keyTerms.definition: The full estimated cost of a year of college, including tuition, fees, housing, food, books, and personal expenses.
A regular cost that stays roughly the same each month, such as rent or a subscription.
A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries, gas, or entertainment.
A plan that matches expected income against expected expenses over a set period of time.
Money set aside and not used for everyday spending, meant to cover unexpected costs.
Spending more money than is available in a checking account, often resulting in a bank fee.

practiceQuestions.question: A student only budgets for tuition and forgets to plan for housing, food, and books. What number should they have looked at instead?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The **cost of attendance** includes every major expense category, not just tuition, and gives a realistic budgeting starting point.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of a variable expense?
choices: Grocery spending that changes week to week
An annual student fee charged every semester
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **variable expense** like groceries changes from month to month, unlike a **fixed expense** that stays roughly constant.

practiceQuestions.question: A student spends freely during the first few weeks of the semester and later has to pay a fee because their checking account balance went negative. What happened?
choices: They lowered their cost of attendance
practiceQuestions.explanation: Spending beyond the available balance causes an **overdraft**, which typically comes with a bank fee.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is it useful to set aside a small emergency fund even on a tight student budget?
choices: It guarantees a higher credit score
It covers unexpected costs without disrupting the regular budget
It replaces the need for financial aid
It is required by all colleges
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **emergency fund** exists specifically to absorb a surprise expense without throwing off the rest of the **budget**.

lessons.title: Managing Unstructured Time
lessons.summary: High school runs on **external structure** — bells, assigned seats, and teachers checking homework — but college hands students **unstructured time** instead, sometimes with only a few scheduled hours a day. Without a plan, that freedom can quietly become wasted time, which is why building a **self-directed schedule** matters from week one. A practical strategy is **time block**ing: assigning specific chunks of the day to specific tasks, like '2:00-3:30 p.m., econ reading,' instead of a vague plan to 'study later.' It also helps to notice a personal **procrastination trigger** — a habit, like an open group chat, that reliably derails focus — so it can be managed in advance. Many successful students protect a short **weekly planning session** to map out the coming week before it starts.

keyTerms.definition: Open time in a schedule with no assigned activity, common in college compared to a fully scheduled high school day.
A specific chunk of time assigned to a specific task, used to turn vague plans into concrete action.
Schedules and deadlines imposed by someone else, such as a teacher or bell schedule, rather than self-managed.
A daily or weekly plan a student builds and manages independently, without someone else enforcing it.
A specific situation, habit, or environment that reliably leads to avoiding a task.
A regular, short block of time set aside to plan the upcoming week's tasks and priorities.

practiceQuestions.question: A first-year college student has only 12 scheduled class hours a week compared to 35 hours a week in high school. What is the biggest shift they need to manage?
choices: Less external structure and much more unstructured time to plan themselves
No more need to study at all
practiceQuestions.explanation: College removes much of the **external structure** of high school, leaving large amounts of **unstructured time** for the student to manage.

practiceQuestions.question: Instead of writing 'study for chemistry later' in a planner, a student writes '4:00-5:30 p.m., review chemistry chapter 6.' What strategy is this?
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Time block**ing assigns a specific task to a specific window of time, making the plan concrete instead of vague.

practiceQuestions.question: A student notices they always end up scrolling their phone instead of starting homework whenever they sit on their bed to work. What should they call this pattern?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recognizing a **procrastination trigger** allows a student to change the environment, like working at a desk instead of a bed.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a weekly planning session?
choices: To memorize a full semester of assignments at once
To map out the coming week's priorities and tasks before it starts
To replace the need for a degree audit
To avoid all unstructured time entirely
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **weekly planning session** turns a week of open time into a manageable, prioritized plan before it begins.

lessons.title: Self-Care, Stress, and Support Networks
lessons.summary: The pressure of a final year of applications and looming transition can build toward **burnout** — physical and emotional exhaustion from prolonged stress that shows up as fatigue, irritability, or losing motivation for things that used to matter. Catching it early starts with recognizing the warning signs rather than pushing through until a crisis. A healthy **coping strategy**, like exercise, sleep, or talking with a trusted friend, works far better than avoidance, like overworking or withdrawing completely. Every college has a **support network** built in, including a **counseling center** offering low-cost sessions and peer mentors, but these only help if a student practices **help-seeking** — reaching out before things become overwhelming. Using a **campus resource** now, in a lower-stakes moment, makes it easier to use one later.

keyTerms.definition: A state of physical and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged stress, often marked by low motivation and irritability.
A healthy habit or action used to manage stress, such as exercise, sleep, or talking with someone trusted.
The group of people, both personal and institutional, a student can turn to for help during difficult times.
A service provided by a college, such as tutoring, advising, or counseling, usually available at low or no cost.
A campus office offering mental health support, often including free or low-cost sessions for enrolled students.
The active choice to reach out for support before a problem becomes a crisis.

practiceQuestions.question: A student notices they feel exhausted, irritable, and no longer excited about activities they used to enjoy. What might they be experiencing?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Exhaustion, irritability, and lost motivation are classic warning signs of **burnout**.

practiceQuestions.question: Which of the following is a healthy coping strategy for managing stress?
choices: Withdrawing completely from friends and activities
Ignoring the stress and working even longer hours
Talking with a trusted friend and getting consistent sleep
Skipping all meals to save time
practiceQuestions.explanation: A genuine **coping strategy** actively manages stress, unlike avoidance behaviors that tend to make burnout worse.

practiceQuestions.question: A student is struggling but waits until finals week, in full crisis, to consider getting help. What habit would have made this easier to manage?
choices: Practicing help-seeking earlier, before things became overwhelming
Waiting even longer to see if it resolves on its own
Only talking to people outside the support network
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Help-seeking** works best as an early habit, not a last resort reserved for a full crisis.

practiceQuestions.question: What is a counseling center an example of?
choices: A campus resource available to support student mental health
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **counseling center** is one of many **campus resource**s built into the **support network** available to enrolled students.

lessons.title: Exploring Careers and Choosing (or Changing) a Major
lessons.summary: Choosing a major shouldn't be a guess — it should be grounded in real **labor market research**, looking at what jobs a major leads to, expected salaries, and demand in the field. One of the most useful tools for this is the **informational interview**: a short, informal conversation with someone already working in a field of interest, asked to learn about their day-to-day work rather than to request a job. It's also normal to enter college with **undeclared status**, taking time to explore before committing. If a student later realizes a **major-career mismatch** — the major doesn't lead where they want to go — the fix is identifying which **transferable skill**s already gained carry over to a better-fitting **career pathway**.

keyTerms.definition: A short, informal conversation with someone in a field of interest, used to learn about their work rather than to ask for a job.
A general sequence of roles and experiences that lead toward a type of career over time.
A situation where a student's declared major does not actually lead to the career they want.
Investigating real data on job demand, salary, and growth for careers connected to a potential major.
Being enrolled in college without having committed to a specific major yet.
An ability, like writing or problem-solving, that applies across many different majors and careers.

practiceQuestions.question: A student wants to learn what a typical day is like for a nurse practitioner before committing to that path. What should they do?
choices: Request an informational interview with someone in that role
Only read the job's salary online
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **informational interview** gives a firsthand, realistic view of a career that research alone can't provide.

practiceQuestions.question: A student realizes halfway through their major that it doesn't actually lead to the career they want. What is the best next step?
choices: Identify transferable skills already gained and research a better-fitting career pathway
Ignore the mismatch and hope it works out
Blame the college for the mismatch
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recognizing a **major-career mismatch** early allows a student to apply their **transferable skill**s toward a more fitting **career pathway** instead of starting over.

practiceQuestions.question: Why is entering college with undeclared status a reasonable choice for some students?
choices: It disqualifies a student from financial aid
It allows time to explore options through research and informational interviews before committing
It means the student cannot graduate on time under any circumstances
It is only allowed at community colleges
practiceQuestions.explanation: **Undeclared status** gives a student room to explore through **labor market research** and conversations before locking in a major.

practiceQuestions.question: Before committing to a major, a student looks up job growth projections and typical starting salaries in that field. What is this an example of?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reviewing job growth and salary data is a core part of **labor market research** used to make an informed major decision.

lessons.title: Networking and Professional Communication
lessons.summary: **Networking** is the ongoing practice of building genuine professional relationships, and it starts with knowing how to introduce yourself well. A strong **professional introduction** states your name, your current role or goal, and a specific reason for the conversation, rather than a vague greeting. Much of this connecting happens over email, so every student should know how to write a **professional email**: a clear **subject line**, a respectful greeting, a short request, and a signature — not a casual text-style message. A well-built **LinkedIn profile**, with an appropriate photo and real experience listed, becomes part of a student's professional presence and should be treated with the same care as any other piece of a **digital footprint**, since employers check it before meeting a candidate.

keyTerms.definition: The ongoing practice of building and maintaining genuine professional relationships over time.
A brief, clear self-introduction stating your name, role or goal, and reason for reaching out.
A written message that uses a clear subject line, respectful tone, and specific request, appropriate for workplace or academic communication.
The short line summarizing an email's purpose, seen before the message is opened.
An online professional profile listing a person's experience, education, and skills, used for networking and job searching.
The overall trail of information about a person that exists online, including social media and professional profiles.

practiceQuestions.question: A student emails a professor's contact for advice with the subject line 'hey' and no greeting or signature. What is the biggest problem with this email?
choices: It is not written as a professional email with a clear subject line and respectful tone
It was sent too early in the day
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **professional email** needs a clear **subject line**, respectful greeting, and proper closing to be taken seriously.

practiceQuestions.question: What should a strong professional introduction include?
choices: Only a first name and nothing else
Name, current role or goal, and a specific reason for the conversation
A list of every class the student has taken
practiceQuestions.explanation: A clear **professional introduction** gives the listener exactly what they need to understand who you are and why you're talking.

practiceQuestions.question: A recruiter searches a student's name online before an interview and finds an outdated, incomplete LinkedIn profile alongside public social media posts. What does this reflect?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Everything discoverable about a person online, including their **LinkedIn profile**, forms their **digital footprint**.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the primary purpose of networking?
choices: Collecting as many contacts as possible with no follow-up
Building genuine, ongoing professional relationships over time
Only useful once a person already has a job
Asking every contact for a job immediately
practiceQuestions.explanation: True **networking** is about sustained, genuine relationships, not one-time transactional requests.

lessons.title: Internships, Early Experience, and Workplace Professionalism
lessons.summary: An **internship** gives a student real exposure to a career field before fully committing to it, and even a short or unpaid version counts as valuable **early experience** on a resume. Success in any workplace depends as much on **soft skill**s — communication, teamwork, reliability — as on technical ability, and employers consistently rank them as top hiring factors. Learning basic **workplace norm**s matters immediately: showing up on time demonstrates **punctuality**, which employers read as respect and reliability, while communicating appropriately shows a student understands the environment. Just as important is learning to receive **professional feedback** without becoming defensive, treating a supervisor's correction as useful information for growth — a mindset that separates strong interns from ones who don't get asked back.

keyTerms.definition: A structured, often short-term work experience in a professional field, which may be paid or unpaid.
Any work, volunteer, or project experience gained before entering a full-time career, valuable for building a resume.
An unwritten or written expectation for behavior in a professional setting, such as punctuality or appropriate communication.
A non-technical ability like communication, teamwork, or reliability that matters across nearly every job.
Consistently arriving on time, viewed by employers as a sign of respect and reliability.
Constructive input from a supervisor or colleague meant to help someone improve their work.

practiceQuestions.question: An employer says soft skills are one of the top factors in hiring decisions, even above technical ability in many cases. Which of these is an example of a soft skill?
choices: Knowledge of a specific software program
practiceQuestions.explanation: A **soft skill** like teamwork or communication applies across nearly every job, unlike a narrow technical skill.

practiceQuestions.question: A student's supervisor points out a mistake in their work and offers a way to fix it. What is the most professional response?
choices: Becoming defensive and arguing the point
Listening, thanking them, and applying the feedback to improve
practiceQuestions.explanation: Treating **professional feedback** as useful information for growth, rather than personal criticism, is a key **workplace norm**.

practiceQuestions.question: Why might even a short, unpaid internship still be valuable for a student's resume?
choices: It counts as early experience that demonstrates real exposure to a career field
Unpaid experience never counts on a resume
It replaces the need for a college degree
It guarantees a full-time job offer
practiceQuestions.explanation: An **internship**, paid or not, still provides genuine **early experience** that strengthens a resume.

practiceQuestions.question: A new intern consistently arrives five minutes early to every shift. What does this demonstrate to their employer?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Consistent **punctuality** signals reliability and respect for the workplace, both valued **workplace norm**s.
